questions.question: What are the most important String methods you should know for interviews?
questions.title: Important String Methods
questions.direct_answer: The core String methods interviewers expect: length, charAt, substring, indexOf, replace, split, trim/strip, toUpperCase/toLowerCase, and isEmpty/isBlank.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical API knowledge and hands-on experience
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Knowing method names but not return types or edge cases (substring end index is exclusive)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Java 11+ additions like strip(), isBlank(), repeat() and explain trim() vs strip() difference

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: Interviewers expect you to know the core String API well enough to use it during a coding problem without hesitation. Here are the methods that come up most.

rows: Throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException if i out of range
end is exclusive — chars start to end-1
Returns -1 if not found, not null
Takes regex — escape special chars like dot

beats.content: Java 11 added strip(), isBlank(), and repeat(). Use strip() over trim() in new code — it handles Unicode whitespace correctly. repeat(n) creates a string repeated n times, useful in coding problems.

sections.hook: Knowing method names is table stakes. Interviewers catch candidates on return types and edge cases — especially substring's exclusive end index.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So the String methods you absolutely need to know for fresher interviews:

`length()` — returns number of characters (not characters minus 1; it's not 0-indexed).

`charAt(int index)` — returns the char at that position. Index 0 to length-1.

`substring(int start)` and `substring(int start, int end)` — extracts a portion. The end index is EXCLUSIVE, which is a very common source of bugs and interview trick questions.

`indexOf(String s)` — first occurrence, returns -1 if not found.

`replace(char old, char new)` and `replace(String old, String new)` — replaces all occurrences.

`split(String regex)` — splits into an array. Note it takes a regex so you need to escape special chars like `.`.

`trim()` removes leading/trailing ASCII whitespace. `strip()` (Java 11+) removes Unicode whitespace. Prefer strip() in modern code.

`toUpperCase()`/`toLowerCase()` — case conversion.

`isEmpty()` — true if length is 0. `isBlank()` (Java 11+) — true if empty or only whitespace.

sections.title: Key Points
content: length() not length-1
substring end index is exclusive
split() takes regex
trim() = ASCII whitespace; strip() = Unicode whitespace (Java 11+)
isEmpty() = length 0; isBlank() = only whitespace (Java 11+)

questions.question: How does String.format() work and when do you use it?
questions.title: String.format()
questions.direct_answer: String.format() creates a formatted string using format specifiers like %s for strings, %d for integers, and %f for floats.

interviewer_intent.testing: String manipulation and output formatting knowledge
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using + concatenation for complex formatted output instead of format()
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention formatted() instance method (Java 15+) and printf() alternative

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: String.format() builds a string by replacing placeholders with actual values. Think of it as a template — you write the shape of the output once and fill in the blanks at runtime.

content: %s — any object, calls toString()
%d — integer
%f — floating point; %.2f for two decimal places
%n — platform-independent newline
%05d — zero-padded integer five characters wide

beats.content: Use format() when you're mixing several values into one string — it's more readable than chaining + operators. Java 15 added formatted() as an instance method: "Hello %s".formatted(name) — same result, slightly cleaner. Note: format() returns a String without printing. System.out.printf() prints directly using the same syntax.

sections.hook: Complex string building with + quickly becomes unreadable. String.format() keeps the structure visible and the values separate.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So String.format() is like printf() from C — it lets you build strings with placeholders that get replaced with actual values. The common format specifiers are: %s for any Object (calls toString()), %d for integers, %f for floats (%.2f for 2 decimal places), %n for a newline (platform-independent), %b for boolean.

Example: `String.format("Hello %s, you scored %d out of 100", name, score)` produces 'Hello Alice, you scored 87 out of 100'.

format() is especially useful when you have complex strings mixing multiple values, or when you want to control number formatting like `%.2f` for currency or `%05d` for zero-padded numbers.

In Java 15+, you can also call `"template %s".formatted(value)` as an instance method — same behavior, slightly cleaner syntax. For logging, most frameworks accept format strings natively so you don't need String.format() there.

sections.title: Key Points
content: %s = string, %d = int, %f = float, %n = newline, %b = boolean
%.2f for 2 decimal places, %05d for zero-padded
Returns a new String (doesn't print)
Java 15+: "template %s".formatted(val) instance method
Not needed in logging — loggers have their own %s/{} syntax

questions.question: How does String.split() work and what are the common pitfalls?
questions.title: String.split() Pitfalls
questions.direct_answer: split() takes a regex pattern, returns a String array — common pitfalls are that special regex chars like . and | must be escaped, and trailing empty strings are dropped by default.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical String manipulation and regex awareness
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using split(".") which splits on every character because . is a regex wildcard
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the limit parameter and trailing empty string behavior

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: The biggest trap: split() takes a regex, not a plain string. Dot in regex means 'any character'. So split(".") splits on every single character, not on literal dots. You need split("\\.") to match a literal dot.

content: Pipe | also has regex meaning — escape as "\\|" for literal pipe
Pattern.quote(delimiter) safely escapes any special characters
Trailing empty strings are dropped by default: "a,,b,,.split(",") gives [a, , b]
split(",", -1) keeps all trailing empty strings
split(",", 2) gives at most 2 parts — everything after the first comma goes into element 1

sections.hook: split(".") is one of the most common Java bugs in the wild. It matches every character, not literal dots.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So split() takes a regex pattern, not a plain string. This catches a lot of people. The most common mistake is `s.split(".")` expecting to split on dot — but in regex, dot means 'any character', so this splits every character. You need `s.split("\\.")` to escape the dot for regex.

Same issue with pipe: `s.split("|")` doesn't work — use `s.split("\\|")`. For simple fixed-string splitting, `Pattern.quote(delimiter)` safely escapes special characters.

Another pitfall: by default, trailing empty strings are discarded. `"a,,b,,".split(",")` gives `["a", "", "b"]` — the trailing empty strings after the last comma are dropped. Use `split(",", -1)` to keep them.

The limit parameter controls max splits: `split(",", 2)` gives at most 2 parts — everything after the first comma goes into the second element.

sections.title: Key Points
content: split() takes a REGEX, not a plain string
"." matches everything — escape as "\\." for literal dot
Pattern.quote(str) for safe literal splitting
Trailing empty strings dropped by default
split(regex, -1) to keep trailing empty strings
split(regex, n) for at most n parts

questions.question: Why is the end index in String.substring() exclusive?
questions.title: substring() End Index
questions.direct_answer: substring(start, end) returns characters at indices start to end-1 — length of result equals end minus start, which is mathematically consistent with all Java range APIs.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating end index as inclusive — common source of StringIndexOutOfBoundsException
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that subList, Arrays.copyOfRange, and all Java range APIs use the same exclusive-end convention

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: substring(start, end) returns characters at indices start through end-1. The end index is not included. So substring(2, 5) gives characters at positions 2, 3, and 4 — three characters.

content: Result length always equals end minus start — clean and predictable
substring(0, s.length()) returns a full copy of the string
To get the last 3 characters: s.substring(s.length() - 3)
This convention is consistent across all Java range APIs: List.subList(from, to), Arrays.copyOfRange(arr, from, to)

beats.content: The exclusive end makes math simpler. If you want characters from index 2 to index 4 inclusive, end minus start = 3 characters — which matches the result length exactly. Treating end as inclusive would break that formula.

sections.hook: substring(2, 5) gives three characters — not four. The end index is exclusive. This trips up candidates every interview season.

sections.title: Key Points
content: substring(2, 5) → chars at index 2, 3, 4 (NOT 5)
Result length = end - start
substring(0, s.length()) = full copy
Consistent with: List.subList(from,to), Arrays.copyOfRange(arr,from,to)
To get last 3 chars: s.substring(s.length() - 3)

questions.question: What is the difference between replace() and replaceAll() in Java?
questions.title: replace() vs replaceAll()
questions.direct_answer: replace() takes a literal character or string; replaceAll() takes a regex pattern — use replace() for simple substitutions to avoid regex metacharacter surprises.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using replaceAll('.', 'X') thinking it replaces literal dots — dot in regex matches everything
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show that replace() is the safe default unless regex is actually needed

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: The name replaceAll() sounds like it replaces every occurrence — which it does. But the key difference from replace() is what the first argument means.

The trap: replaceAll(".", "X") replaces every character because dot is a regex wildcard. To replace actual dots, use replace(".", "X") — no escaping needed, it's treated as a literal. Default rule: use replace() unless you actually need regex power.

sections.hook: replaceAll and replace both replace all occurrences. The difference is whether the first argument is a regex — and that changes everything.

sections.title: Key Points
content: replace(char, char) or replace(String, String) — literal, replaces all
replaceAll(regex, str) — regex pattern, replaces all matches
replaceFirst(regex, str) — regex, replaces first match
Trap: replaceAll(".", "X") replaces EVERY character (. = any in regex)
Safe dot replace: replace(".", "dot") not replaceAll("." , "dot")
